title: Saint Alder's Rising Revisited
premise: When the coffin of Saint Alder's founder, Aldous Wren, is opened for a bicentennial reinterment, it contains only river stones and a 1902 letter addressed 'to whoever finally asks.' Rosalind Eriksen, the hotel concierge whose quiet observations have solved a dozen small town mysteries, realizes the town's founding myth is a cover for a disappearance the Wren family buried along with the empty coffin. As she follows the letter's clues, she uncovers that the current mayor, Eleanor Wren, has been quietly destroying records to protect a family secret: Aldous never existed as remembered—he was an identity stolen by a runaway woman whose descendants, including Rosalind's own grandmother, kept the pact. In the end, Rosalind must choose between exposing the truth that would shatter Saint Alder's identity and Eleanor's quiet offer of belonging, and she chooses a third path: publishing the real founder's story as fiction, closing the case while keeping the town—and her place in it—intact.
about_author: Oscar Hartwell is the pen name of a former night-desk clerk who spent a decade listening to small-town secrets through hotel lobby conversations. Hartwell writes mysteries where the real crime is what a community agrees to forget.

chapters.title: The Weight of River Stones
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. During the bicentennial exhumation, Rosalind watches the crowd from the hotel lobby and notices what no one else does: the coffin is too light, the mayor's hands too steady. When river stones and a sealed letter are revealed, the town reels. Rosalind pockets a photograph that slips from the mayor's coat, torn between professional detachment and the thrill of finally being seen. Beat: the invisible observer is pulled into the light.

chapters.title: A Letter to Whoever Finally Asks
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. Deciphering the 1902 letter, Rosalind traces Aldous Wren's paper trail to a boarding house ledger and discovers the founder was a woman named Ada Wrenley, whose portrait hangs mislabeled in the town archive. Eleanor Wren warns her off with unsettling warmth, offering Rosalind a promotion and a place in the town's inner circle. Rosalind finds her grandmother's name in the ledger. Beat: loyalty to the town begins to war with the truth.

chapters.title: What the River Kept
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind, with a brief interlude in Ada Wrenley's 1902 diary voice. Following the letter's final clue to a drowned ferry landing, Rosalind recovers Ada's diary proving the identity theft was an escape, not a crime—and that Rosalind's grandmother was Ada's confidante. Eleanor confronts her at the landing, confessing generations of Wrens have protected the myth. When the diary is nearly destroyed, Rosalind realizes someone else has been following her. Beat: the case turns personal and dangerous.

chapters.title: The Story We Agree To Keep
chapters.summary: POV Rosalind. At the reinterment ceremony, the stalker—town historian Miles, Ada's other descendant—threatens to expose everything cruelly. Rosalind outmaneuvers him by publishing Ada's story herself as historical fiction, credited to 'Oscar Hartwell,' reclaiming the narrative on her own terms. Eleanor accepts the compromise; the town gets its ceremony, Ada gets her name. Rosalind, no longer invisible, chooses to stay. Beat: truth and belonging reconciled, the case closed.
